title: Stochastic Gene Expression: Master Equation
markdown: ## What this covers A single gene switches on and produces messenger RNA at a constant rate; each mRNA is translated into protein before it is degraded; the protein itself is stable. This chapter takes that simplest possible model of gene expression and asks every question that can be asked of it: the mean mRNA and protein numbers, the growth rate of the population, and — the harder half — the full probability *distributions* of mRNA number, protein bursts per mRNA, and protein number in the cell. It assumes the deterministic picture of transcription and translation (synthesis and degradation rates) and builds the stochastic description, the master equation, from scratch. It also revisits the Sunney Xie bacterial gene-expression paper discussed earlier in the course, and points forward to the master equation, the Fokker–Planck approximation and the Gillespie algorithm covered in the following lecture. ## The model and its four rate constants The gene is assumed always active — no repressor is bound, or if one is binding and unbinding it is fast enough that the process still looks first-order. Two species, mRNA and protein, each with a synthesis rate and a degradation rate: - $S_m$ — synthesis (transcription) rate of mRNA - $\delta_m$ — degradation rate of mRNA - $S_p$ — synthesis (translation) rate of protein, per mRNA - $\delta_p$ — degradation rate of protein This is a reasonable description of gene expression in bacteria when the gene is in an active state, and it is the model behind the Sunney Xie paper on bursting gene expression discussed earlier in the course. A first point worth being careful about: nothing here has been non-dimensionalized. There is no step where "the unit of time" is set to the cell cycle, or to a lifetime, by fiat — $S_m,\delta_m, S_p,\delta_p$ are still given in physical units (seconds, minutes, hours), and $\delta t = 1$ is not automatically one cell cycle. Non-dimensionalizing would come from *setting* one of these rates to $1$, and that has not been done. **Convention used throughout:** many of the quantities below come out as a ratio of two of these four rates, so keep them straight: $S_m,\ \delta_m,\ S_p,\ \delta_p$ — synthesis over degradation, mRNA then protein. ## Effective degradation and the growth rate of the population Take the protein to be *stable*: no active degradation, so its true physical degradation rate is $0$. Even so, if the cell population is dividing and growing, the protein still disappears from an individual cell — by dilution. Write $$ \delta_p^{\text{eff}} = \gamma_{\text{growth}} + \delta_p^{\text{true}}, $$ where $\gamma_{\text{growth}}$ is the exponential growth rate of the cell population. For a stable protein, $\delta_p^{\text{true}} = 0$, so the *effective* degradation rate of the protein is just $\gamma_{\text{growth}}$: watching a population of cells grow exponentially in a spectrophotometer, the rate of that growth is exactly the effective degradation rate you would assign the protein. The intuition: if you stop making the protein and the number of cells doubles, the concentration in each cell must fall by a factor of two purely from dilution — that fall *is* an effective degradation, with no chemistry involved. More generally — whether or not the protein is stable — $\delta_p^{\text{eff}}$ is always this sum of a true (chemical) degradation rate and a dilution term set by the growth rate; "stable" is just the special case where the chemical part vanishes and the effective rate reduces to the growth rate. mRNA typically has a genuinely faster degradation rate than the dilution term contributes, so for mRNA the effective and true degradation rates are close; proteins typically live much longer than mRNAs, which is part of why treating the protein as stable (only diluted, not chemically degraded) is a reasonable simplification. ## Mean numbers: working through the model level by level Each of the following is a **mean**, derived from the deterministic picture — birth rate against death rate of the relevant species — before anything stochastic is introduced. **Mean mRNA per cell.** Made at rate $S_m$, with a lifetime $1/\delta_m$, so $$ \langle m \rangle = \frac{S_m}{\delta_m}. $$ This holds regardless of whether the physical degradation rate dominates the dilution term or not — the formula does not care which piece of $\delta_m$ is doing the work, only that $\delta_m$ is the *effective* rate. **Mean protein produced per mRNA.** Once an mRNA exists, it is a competition between the rate at which it fires off proteins, $S_p$, and the rate at which it is degraded, $\delta_m$: $$ \langle n_{\text{protein per mRNA}} \rangle = \frac{S_p}{\delta_m}. $$ If $S_p = \delta_m$, on average about one protein is made before the mRNA is degraded; if $S_p = 2\delta_m$, about two. This is a statement about *production only*, not about the ratio of steady-state protein to mRNA concentrations in the cell (which would instead be $S_p/\delta_p$, since it is comparing two things that are both present, not asking how many protein molecules a single mRNA generates before dying). **Mean protein per cell.** Multiply the mean number of mRNA in the cell by the mean protein produced per mRNA... but that double-counts the roles of $S_m,\delta_m$. Cleanly: $$ \langle p \rangle = \frac{S_m}{\delta_m}\cdot\frac{S_p}{\delta_p} = \frac{S_m S_p}{\delta_m \delta_p}. $$ The reasoning volunteered in the lecture: this is the same logic as the mean mRNA number — a production rate over a degradation rate — except the "production rate" for protein, per mRNA, does not care about concentration; it is just (mean number of mRNA present) $\times$ ($S_p$), and that whole thing is degraded at rate $\delta_p$, giving $S_p/\delta_p$ if there were exactly one mRNA, then scaled up by the mean mRNA number. **Mean mRNA produced per cell cycle.** Distinct from the mean number of mRNA sitting in the cell at any instant — this asks how many are *produced* over one generation, ignoring the $\log 2$ factor that would convert a growth rate into a doubling time: $$ \langle m_{\text{per cycle}} \rangle \approx \frac{S_m}{\delta_p}, $$ because $\delta_p$ (for a stable protein, equal to the growth rate) sets the cell division rate, and cell generation time is $\log 2$ divided by that rate. This quantity is the same thing as the mean number of protein "bursts" observed per cell cycle in the Sunney Xie paper. It is easy to conflate this with the mean mRNA *in* the cell, $S_m/\delta_m$ — they are different questions with, typically, very different numerical answers, because $\delta_m \gg \delta_p$ (mRNA degrades much faster than the cell divides). In Xie's data there was just over one mRNA produced per cell cycle, but the mean number of mRNA present in the cell at any moment was around $1/30$ of that, because the mRNA lifetime was only about $1.5$ minutes. ## Two distributions that are both Poisson, and are not the same Poisson Two quantities turn out to be Poisson-distributed, and it is easy to think this must be the *same* distribution appearing twice — it is not; they have different means. **Number of mRNA produced per cell cycle** is Poisson with mean $S_m/\delta_p$. A Poisson distribution is exactly what arises when there is some constant probability per unit time of an event, and the count is taken over a fixed time window — here, transcription events over one cell cycle. **Number of mRNA present in the cell at a given instant** is also Poisson — but with mean $S_m/\delta_m$, which is much smaller because $\delta_m \gg \delta_p$. In a typical bacterial condition matching Xie's data, this means a cell would typically have *no* mRNA present at all, even though on the order of one mRNA is produced (and degraded) per generation. The lecture flags this explicitly as confusing on first encounter — "there's probably a reason they're the same [both Poisson], but it's not immediately obvious" — but stresses that they are numerically different Poisson distributions and should not be conflated. ## The size of a single protein burst is geometric Fix attention on one mRNA and ask: how many protein molecules does it produce in total before it is degraded? Not the mean — the whole distribution. Model it as a two-state loop: from the "mRNA present" state, either (a) the mRNA degrades, at rate $\delta_m$, ending the process, or (b) a protein is synthesized, at rate $S_p$, and the process loops back to "mRNA present" having produced one more protein. Define $$ \rho = \frac{S_p}{S_p + \delta_m}, $$ the probability that, from the mRNA-present state, the *next* event is another round of protein synthesis rather than degradation. To get exactly $n$ proteins, the process must take the synthesis branch $n$ times in a row and then the degradation branch once, so $$ P(n) = \rho^n (1-\rho), $$ a **geometric distribution**. It is normalized correctly: $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \rho^n(1-\rho) = (1-\rho)\cdot \frac{1}{1-\rho} = 1$. Its mean is $$ \langle n \rangle = \frac{\rho}{1-\rho}, $$ which diverges as $\rho \to 1$ — makes sense, since $\rho \to 1$ means the mRNA essentially always synthesizes another protein rather than ever degrading. This construction assumes the successive rounds are independent — a strong assumption (a student pushed back on this in class, e.g. whether mRNAs actually get "caught" in ribosomes) — and the lecturer's answer is the general methodological point: **write down the simplest model first, measure, and check whether it explains the data; only then add complexity.** In Xie's *E. coli* data, the geometric distribution with a single free parameter (mean protein burst size around $4$ or $5$) fit well, meaning whatever more complicated biology might in principle be happening was not *significant* in that condition. A caution about the literature: there are several inequivalent conventions for "the geometric distribution" — depending on whether the parameter is defined as the probability of continuing or the probability of terminating, and on whether $n$ counts proteins produced or counts loop passes including or excluding the first one. Formulas that look alike can differ by a shift or by $\rho \leftrightarrow 1-\rho$; check which convention is in use before matching an equation from memory. One more distinction, raised directly in class discussion: this geometric distribution describes proteins produced *per mRNA*, over that mRNA's entire (finite) lifetime. It is not defined if there is no mRNA degradation at all ($\delta_m \to 0$): then a single mRNA produces infinitely many proteins and the "per mRNA" question has no finite answer. What *would* be Poisson in that zeroth-order limit is a related but different question — the number of proteins produced *per unit time* (rather than per mRNA), which reduces to a plain Poisson counting process once mRNA number itself is Poisson and degradation is switched off. ## The master equation for mRNA number Having the mean and the per-mRNA burst distribution still does not answer the harder question: what is the full probability distribution of the number of mRNA molecules present in the cell? For that, build the master equation — the tool for turning a single deterministic ODE into an (infinite) family of equations for probabilities. The deterministic picture is the simplest possible ODE: $$ \dot m = S_m - \delta_m m, $$ with the unique fixed point $m_{\text{eq}} = S_m/\delta_m$ and relaxation timescale $1/\delta_m$: a trajectory started away from equilibrium approaches it exponentially with that characteristic time, from above or below. Now build the stochastic analogue. Define states $M_n$: the state in which there are exactly $n$ mRNA molecules present, for $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ (you cannot go below $0$). The system moves between neighboring states $M_n \leftrightarrow M_{n+1}$ at rates $f_n$ (forward, $n \to n+1$) and $g_n$ (backward, from $n$ to $n-1$; written $g_{n+1}$ when leaving $M_{n+1}$ for $M_n$). For every state $n \ge 1$, probability is lost by leaving (at rate $f_n + g_n$) and gained from the two neighbors: $$ \frac{d P(M_n)}{dt} = f_{n-1} P(M_{n-1}) + g_{n+1} P(M_{n+1}) - \big(f_n + g_n\big) P(M_n), $$ with the boundary case $n=0$ missing the terms that would come from the left. This is the master equation: one differential equation per value of $n$, so a single simple ODE has become an infinite family of coupled ODEs, each a bit more complicated than the original. That is the price of asking for the whole distribution rather than just the mean — but it buys two things: it is a tool for exact analytic calculation, and it is a principled way to set up a stochastic simulation (a "weigh station" en route to something like the Gillespie algorithm, covered next lecture). For this model, the rates are simple: $$ f_n = S_m \quad\text{(constant — synthesis doesn't care how many mRNA are already present)}, \qquad g_n = \delta_m\, n \quad\text{(more mRNA present means more can degrade)}. $$ **Detailed balance at equilibrium.** At steady state, the net flux across every single arrow in the chain must vanish — not just the total probability of each state — because otherwise there would be a systematic drift around the chain and no true equilibrium. So for every $n$: $$ f_n\, P(M_n) = g_{n+1}\, P(M_{n+1}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{P(M_{n+1})}{P(M_n)} = \frac{f_n}{g_{n+1}} = \frac{S_m}{\delta_m (n+1)}. $$ Unrolling this recursion from $P(M_0)$: $$ P(M_1) = \frac{S_m}{\delta_m} P(M_0), \qquad P(M_2) = \frac{S_m}{\delta_m}\cdot\frac{S_m}{2\delta_m} P(M_0) = \frac{1}{2!}\Big(\frac{S_m}{\delta_m}\Big)^2 P(M_0), $$ and in general, writing $\lambda \equiv S_m/\delta_m$, $$ P(M_n) = \frac{\lambda^n}{n!} P(M_0). $$ Normalizing, $\sum_n P(M_n) = P(M_0)\sum_n \lambda^n/n! = P(M_0)\, e^{\lambda} = 1$, so $P(M_0) = e^{-\lambda}$ and $$ P(M_n) = \frac{\lambda^n}{n!} e^{-\lambda}, $$ a **Poisson distribution** with mean $\lambda = S_m/\delta_m$ — exactly the deterministic equilibrium mean computed earlier. The general statement this illustrates: a constant creation rate and a per-item degradation rate, for a single species, always give a Poisson distribution at steady state. **Mean of the stochastic process equals the deterministic trajectory — here, but not always.** Because $f_n$ and $g_n$ are both *linear* in $n$ for this model, the expectation $\langle m(t) \rangle$ obtained from the master equation obeys exactly the same equation as the deterministic ODE, at every time, not just at equilibrium. A single stochastic trajectory is jagged — it is discrete and noisy even once it has settled near equilibrium — and the deterministic curve is what you get by averaging infinitely many such trajectories together. This coincidence between the mean of the stochastic dynamics and the deterministic dynamics is special to *linear* birth–death rates; if $f_n$ or $g_n$ were nonlinear in $n$, the mean of the stochastic process would in general deviate from the deterministic solution. ## What is known so far, and the harder question left over By this point in the model three distributions have been pinned down: - number of mRNA present in the cell at steady state — **Poisson**, mean $S_m/\delta_m$; - number of mRNA produced per cell cycle — a **different Poisson**, mean $\approx S_m/\delta_p$; - number of proteins produced per mRNA (one burst) — **geometric**, mean $S_p/\delta_m$. None of this makes it obvious what the distribution of protein number *in the cell* looks like — knowing that a single burst is geometric does not immediately give the shape of the sum of many random bursts arriving during a cell cycle. (Polled directly in class: is it "obvious" what this distribution is, given everything derived so far? The answer volunteered was no.) ## The protein-number distribution: gamma, the continuous analogue of a sum of geometrics The full discrete derivation is harder than the mRNA case and was not carried out in class (the continuous version is already noticeably harder; the discrete version — the negative binomial, first obtained by Paulsson — is harder still). Instead: reason about it as a convolution and quote the continuous limit. The idea: over one cell cycle, the number of protein *bursts* is Poisson-distributed with mean $a$ (the same $a$ as the mean number of mRNA produced per cell cycle, from earlier). Each burst contributes a geometrically-distributed number of proteins with mean burst size $b = S_p/\delta_m$. Just as the exponential distribution is the continuous approximation to the geometric, the sum of $a$ independent exponential ("continuized geometric") burst sizes converges to a **gamma distribution**: $$ p \sim \Gamma(a, b), $$ with two parameters — $a$, the mean number of bursts per cell cycle, and $b$, the mean burst size — matching the fact that a Poisson needs only one parameter but a gamma needs two. Its mean and variance: $$ \langle p \rangle = ab, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(p) = ab^2. $$ (Sunney Xie has a PRL paper deriving the continuous gamma-distribution result directly; Paulsson derived the underlying discrete negative-binomial distribution earlier still.) **Why a sum of exponentials looks like this.** A single burst (one exponential, scale $b$) is peaked at $0$ — the most likely burst size from a single mRNA is zero proteins, which matches the geometric result that $P(n)$ is largest at $n=0$ whenever $\rho<1$. Summing two independent draws (a convolution) shifts the peak away from $0$ and produces a distribution that rises linearly near the origin; summing three makes it rise quadratically near the origin, and so on — the distribution moves from being peaked at zero to being peaked at some positive value as more bursts accumulate. In the limit of many bursts ($a$ large), the gamma distribution converges to a **Gaussian** — an instance of the central limit theorem: a well-behaved distribution, sampled from and summed many times, converges to normal. **Why the Poisson itself becomes Gaussian for large mean.** A parallel argument, worked through directly in class: if a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ over some interval gives count $X_1 \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, and an independent identical process over an equal further interval gives $X_2 \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, then $X_1+X_2$ — counting the same process over twice the time — must itself be Poisson, and since means always add for independent variables, $X_1+X_2 \sim \text{Poisson}(2\lambda)$. Stack $k$ such intervals: the sum is $\text{Poisson}(k\lambda)$. But a Poisson is a well-behaved distribution, and by the central limit theorem a sum of $k$ independent draws from it must approach a Gaussian as $k$ grows — so a Poisson with large mean has to look Gaussian. (A student's discrete objection is worth keeping: a Poisson can never go negative, and for small $\lambda$ that constraint visibly piles probability up near $0$; only once $\lambda$ is large enough — as a rule of thumb, once $\lambda \gtrsim 100$ — does the distribution have enough room on both sides of its mean to look symmetric and Gaussian.) ## Two loose ends from the discussion **Deviations seen in real data.** In Xie's *E. coli* measurements, mRNA production was not quite a single constant-rate Poisson process over the whole cell cycle: bursting rate depended on cell-cycle stage, because a longer cell (further along toward division) may already carry two copies of the gene rather than one, and so a higher transcription rate. This does not break the Poisson conclusion, though — a Poisson process with rate $\lambda_1$ over part of the cycle, followed by an independent Poisson process with rate $\lambda_2$ over the rest, still sums to a Poisson (with mean $\lambda_1+\lambda_2$, not necessarily the naive single-rate mean); adding Poissons always gives back a Poisson, whatever the individual rates were. **Going to eukaryotes: gene switching, and why mRNA and protein noise decouple.** Real eukaryotic promoters switch between active and inactive states at some rate, and this breaks the simple picture: the mRNA-number distribution in that case is no longer Poisson at all. (Arjun Raj — author of the review discussed in this course — worked out the exact steady-state solution; it involves products of gamma functions and a confluent hypergeometric function of the first kind, and is not reproduced here.) The qualitative consequence: individual mammalian cells can show *hugely* varying mRNA counts — some cells with almost none, some with a great many — yet protein-number distributions across the same cells are comparatively regular, because the much longer protein lifetime averages over the wild mRNA fluctuations. Switching timescales between active and inactive promoter states vary widely by system: on the order of minutes in some cases, hours in others (particularly relevant for mammalian cells, which may divide only about once a day). ## A biological application: noise-tuning during bacterial competence *Bacillus subtilis*, under starvation or other stresses, can enter a state of competence in which it imports DNA from outside — some of which may be incorporated into its own genome. Competence is mediated by the protein ComK, which positively activates its own expression, producing a positive feedback loop and (as a consequence) bistability: only a small fraction of cells enter the high-ComK, competent state at all. Arjun Raj, Hedia Maamar, and Dave Dubnau studied this system and showed that the fraction of cells entering competence is controlled by *noise*, not by the mean. They varied the transcription rate and the translation rate each by roughly a factor of $2$, in opposite directions, so as to hold $\langle p\rangle = (S_m/\delta_m)(S_p/\delta_p)$ fixed while changing the noise: **increasing the transcription rate $S_m$ and decreasing the translation rate $S_p$ reduces noise** at fixed mean, because noise in this model is driven largely by the size of individual protein bursts ($S_p/\delta_m$) — many small bursts (high $S_m$, low $S_p$) average out more smoothly than a few large ones (low $S_m$, high $S_p$), even though both regimes give the same mean protein level. Experimentally, tuning the rates this way, holding the mean fixed, lowered the noise and reduced the fraction of cells reaching the competent state — direct evidence that the noise itself, not the mean expression level, controls this developmental decision. ## Sources - Transcript: `recordings/03bvgr-vyhq.md` (MIT OCW 8.591J, Systems Biology, Fall 2014), full lecture, timestamps 00:00–1:20:20. None of these were supplied as source material for this chapter. - The lecture also points forward to the next class session's treatment of the master equation in general, the Fokker–Planck approximation, and the Gillespie algorithm — none of which is covered in this transcript.
